The words

Holy, holy, holy! Lord God Almighty!
Early in the morning our song shall rise to Thee;
Holy, holy, holy! merciful and mighty,
God in three Persons, blessed Trinity!

Holy, holy, holy! all the saints adore Thee,
Casting down their golden crowns around the glassy sea;
Cherubim and seraphim falling down before Thee,
Which wert, and art, and evermore shalt be.

Holy, holy, holy! though the darkness hide Thee,
Though the eye of sinful man Thy glory may not see,
Only Thou art holy; there is none beside Thee,
Perfect in power, in love, and purity.

Holy, holy, holy! Lord God Almighty!
All Thy works shall praise Thy name, in earth, and sky, and sea;
Holy, holy, holy! merciful and mighty,
God in three Persons, blessed Trinity!

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum D and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (D).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Reginald Heber, Bishop of Calcutta, wrote this hymn for Trinity Sunday; it was printed in 1826, the year he died. John Bacchus Dykes composed the tune NICAEA for it in 1861, named after the Council of Nicaea.

  • Words (1826): Reginald Heber (1783–1826)
  • Melody (1861): John Bacchus Dykes (1823–1876)

Tune NICAEA by John Bacchus Dykes (1823–1876); words by Reginald Heber (1783–1826).

Questions about Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty

What is the doh of Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty?

In this version, in D major, doh is D. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty start on?

It starts on d (D in D major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty in the public domain?

Yes. Reginald Heber died in 1826, John Bacchus Dykes died in 1876; the words were first published in 1826 and the music in 1861. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
